hardestSegment.transcriptSnippet: Gradient descent is the algorithm we use to find the optimal weights.

segments.transcriptSnippet: Welcome to the first session. Today we start with supervised learning and the concept of regression.
segments.transcriptText: Welcome to the first session. Today we start with supervised learning and the concept of regression. Supervised learning means we have labelled training data — each input has a corresponding output that we want to predict. Regression is a type of supervised learning where the output is a continuous number, not a category. The simplest and most fundamental regression algorithm is linear regression. It models the relationship between input features and the output as a straight line — or more generally, a hyperplane in higher dimensions. The goal is to find the line that best fits the data, in the sense that the total prediction error is minimised. Linear regression is not just historically important — it is still widely used in practice because it is interpretable, fast, and often works surprisingly well.

segments.transcriptSnippet: The linear regression model has the form y-hat equals w0 plus w1 times x1 plus w2 times x2 and so on.
segments.transcriptText: The linear regression model has the form y-hat equals w0 plus w1 times x1 plus w2 times x2 and so on. Here y-hat is the predicted output, x1 through xn are the input features, and w0 through wn are the weights or parameters of the model. w0 is called the bias or intercept term — it allows the line to shift up or down without requiring any input feature to be non-zero. In matrix notation, we write y-hat equals Xw, where X is the design matrix with one row per training example and one column per feature, and w is the weight vector. The design matrix usually has a column of ones prepended to handle the bias term. Learning the model means finding the weight vector w that minimises the prediction error on the training data.

segments.transcriptSnippet: To measure how wrong our predictions are, we use a loss function. For regression the standard choice is mean squared error.
segments.transcriptText: To measure how wrong our predictions are, we use a loss function. For regression the standard choice is mean squared error, or MSE. MSE is the average of the squared differences between the predicted output y-hat and the true output y. We square the differences for two reasons: first, it makes negative and positive errors equally penalised; second, it is mathematically convenient because it is smooth and differentiable. Another common loss is mean absolute error, or MAE, which takes the average of the absolute values of the differences instead of the squares. MAE is more robust to outliers because large errors are not amplified by squaring. The choice of loss function depends on the problem: if outliers in the training data are genuine signal that you want the model to fit, use MSE; if outliers are noise, use MAE.

segments.transcriptSnippet: The closed-form solution to linear regression is called the normal equation.
segments.transcriptText: The closed-form solution to linear regression is called the normal equation. If we write the MSE loss as a function of w, take the derivative, set it to zero, and solve, we get: w equals the inverse of X-transpose-X, multiplied by X-transpose-y. This gives us the exact optimal weights in one step, with no iteration required. However, the normal equation has a critical limitation — inverting the matrix X-transpose-X takes time proportional to the cube of the number of features. When you have millions of features, this becomes computationally infeasible. There is also a numerical stability concern: if X-transpose-X is close to singular — for example because two features are nearly perfectly correlated — the inversion becomes unreliable. For these reasons, in practice the normal equation is only used when the number of features is small, typically in the thousands or fewer.

segments.transcriptSnippet: Regularisation is a technique to prevent overfitting by penalising large weights.
segments.transcriptText: Regularisation is a technique to prevent overfitting by penalising large weights. Without regularisation, a model with many features can memorise the training data — it fits the training examples perfectly but fails on new data. This is called overfitting. Regularisation adds a penalty term to the loss function that grows with the magnitude of the weights. Ridge regression, also called L2 regularisation, adds the sum of squared weights multiplied by a hyperparameter lambda. Lasso regression, also called L1 regularisation, adds the sum of absolute values of the weights. Ridge keeps all features but shrinks their weights toward zero. Lasso can shrink some weights all the way to exactly zero, effectively performing feature selection. Elastic net combines both L1 and L2 penalties. The hyperparameter lambda controls the strength of regularisation — a larger lambda means more shrinkage.

segments.transcriptSnippet: Gradient descent is the algorithm we use to find the optimal weights when the normal equation is too expensive.
segments.transcriptText: Gradient descent is the algorithm we use to find the optimal weights when the normal equation is too expensive. The idea is simple: start with random weights, compute the gradient of the loss with respect to the weights, and take a small step in the opposite direction of the gradient. We repeat this until the weights converge. The size of each step is controlled by the learning rate, also called alpha. If the learning rate is too large, the algorithm overshoots the minimum and may diverge. If it is too small, convergence is slow. In batch gradient descent, we compute the gradient using the entire training set for each update. In stochastic gradient descent, we use a single randomly chosen training example. Mini-batch gradient descent uses a small batch of examples, which is the most common variant in practice. The update rule is: w gets w minus alpha times the gradient of the loss with respect to w.

segments.transcriptSnippet: To evaluate a regression model we look at R-squared, which tells us what fraction of the variance in the output the model explains.
segments.transcriptText: To evaluate a regression model we look at R-squared, also called the coefficient of determination. R-squared tells us what fraction of the variance in the output the model explains. A value of 1 means the model explains all the variance — perfect predictions. A value of 0 means the model does no better than simply predicting the mean of the training targets. A negative value is possible and means the model is worse than predicting the mean. It is important not to over-rely on R-squared: adding more features always increases R-squared on the training set even if those features are noise, because the model can always find a way to use them to better fit the training data. Adjusted R-squared corrects for this by penalising the number of features in the model. When comparing models, we should always evaluate on a held-out test set, not on the training data.

segments.transcriptSnippet: That wraps up session one. Next time we move to logistic regression and classification.
segments.transcriptText: That wraps up session one. Next time we move to logistic regression and classification. To summarise what we covered today: linear regression models a continuous output as a linear function of the inputs. We measure error with MSE or MAE. The normal equation gives a closed-form solution but is expensive for many features. Gradient descent is the scalable alternative. Regularisation with L1 or L2 penalties prevents overfitting. R-squared is the standard evaluation metric. Please complete the assignment and come prepared for the quiz at the start of next session.

hardestSegment.transcriptSnippet: The cross-entropy loss is derived from the principle of maximum likelihood estimation.

segments.transcriptSnippet: Classification is the task of predicting a discrete class label rather than a continuous value.
segments.transcriptText: Classification is the task of predicting a discrete class label rather than a continuous value. For example, predicting whether an email is spam or not spam, whether a tumour is malignant or benign, or which digit a handwritten image represents. Binary classification has two classes. Multi-class classification has more than two. Logistic regression, despite its name, is a classification algorithm. It models the probability that an input belongs to the positive class. The output is always between 0 and 1, which makes it interpretable as a probability. At inference time, we typically predict the positive class if the output probability exceeds 0.5, though this threshold can be adjusted depending on the cost of different types of errors.

segments.transcriptSnippet: The sigmoid function squashes any real number into the range zero to one, making it suitable for producing probabilities.
segments.transcriptText: The sigmoid function squashes any real number into the range zero to one, making it suitable for producing probabilities. The formula is sigma of z equals one divided by one plus e to the power of negative z. When z is very large and positive, sigma approaches one. When z is very large and negative, sigma approaches zero. When z equals zero, sigma equals exactly 0.5. In logistic regression, z is the linear combination of features and weights — the same quantity we computed in linear regression. So the model is: probability of y equals one given x equals sigma of w-transpose-x. The derivative of the sigmoid is especially convenient: sigma-prime of z equals sigma of z times one minus sigma of z. This makes gradient-based optimisation clean.

segments.transcriptSnippet: A decision boundary is the surface in feature space where the model predicts exactly 50 percent probability for each class.
segments.transcriptText: A decision boundary is the surface in feature space where the model predicts exactly 50 percent probability for each class. For logistic regression, the decision boundary is always linear — it is a hyperplane. This is because the boundary occurs where w-transpose-x equals zero, which is a linear equation. This means logistic regression can only separate linearly separable classes. If the true boundary between classes is curved or complex, logistic regression will struggle. However, you can extend logistic regression to non-linear boundaries by adding polynomial features or interaction terms. For example, if you add a feature that is x1 squared, the model can learn a parabolic boundary. This is called feature engineering and is a powerful tool when you have domain knowledge about the shape of the decision boundary.

segments.transcriptSnippet: We cannot use MSE as the loss for logistic regression because the resulting optimisation problem is non-convex.
segments.transcriptText: We cannot use MSE as the loss for logistic regression because the resulting optimisation problem is non-convex — it has many local minima, and gradient descent may get stuck. Instead, we use the binary cross-entropy loss, also called log loss. For a single training example, the log loss is: negative y times log of p-hat, minus one minus y times log of one minus p-hat. Here y is the true label — zero or one — and p-hat is the predicted probability. When y equals one and p-hat is close to one, the loss is close to zero — correct confident prediction. When y equals one but p-hat is close to zero, the loss is very large — the model confidently predicted the wrong class. This asymmetry makes the log loss more sensitive to confident wrong predictions than to uncertain wrong predictions.

segments.transcriptSnippet: The cross-entropy loss is derived from the principle of maximum likelihood estimation.
segments.transcriptText: The cross-entropy loss is derived from the principle of maximum likelihood estimation. If we assume each training example is drawn independently from the same distribution, the likelihood of the training data under our model is the product of p-hat to the power y times one minus p-hat to the power of one minus y, taken over all training examples. Maximising this likelihood is equivalent to maximising its log, which is the log-likelihood. Negating the log-likelihood gives us the cross-entropy loss. This connection to maximum likelihood is important because it gives a principled justification for why log loss is the right loss function to use. It also means that when the model converges, the predicted probabilities are calibrated — a predicted probability of 0.7 really does mean approximately 70 percent of such examples belong to the positive class.

segments.transcriptSnippet: Precision and recall are more informative than accuracy when the classes are imbalanced.
segments.transcriptText: Precision and recall are more informative than accuracy when the classes are imbalanced. Accuracy is the fraction of correctly classified examples. But if 99 percent of emails are not spam, a classifier that always predicts not-spam has 99 percent accuracy — yet it is completely useless. Precision is the fraction of predicted positives that are truly positive. Recall, also called sensitivity, is the fraction of true positives that the model correctly identifies. There is a fundamental tradeoff: lowering the classification threshold increases recall but decreases precision, and vice versa. The F1 score combines precision and recall as their harmonic mean. The ROC curve plots the true positive rate against the false positive rate at all possible thresholds, and the area under the ROC curve — the AUC — summarises model performance across all thresholds.

segments.transcriptSnippet: Multi-class logistic regression extends binary logistic regression using the softmax function.
segments.transcriptText: Multi-class logistic regression extends binary logistic regression using the softmax function. Instead of one weight vector, we have one weight vector per class. The softmax function converts the raw scores — called logits — into a probability distribution over all classes. The softmax of class k is: e to the power of the logit for class k, divided by the sum of e to the power of the logit for all classes. The output probabilities sum to one. The loss function is the categorical cross-entropy, which is the same as binary cross-entropy but generalised to multiple classes. Multi-class logistic regression is sometimes called softmax regression. One alternative approach is one-versus-rest, where you train K binary classifiers — one for each class against all others — and predict the class whose classifier is most confident.

segments.transcriptSnippet: Regularisation in logistic regression works the same way as in linear regression — L2 penalises large weights.
segments.transcriptText: Regularisation in logistic regression works the same way as in linear regression. L2 regularisation adds the sum of squared weights to the loss, which shrinks all weights toward zero and prevents overfitting. L1 regularisation adds the sum of absolute weights and can zero out irrelevant features. In scikit-learn, logistic regression uses L2 regularisation by default, controlled by the hyperparameter C, which is the inverse of lambda — a smaller C means stronger regularisation. One important implementation detail: you should always standardise your features before fitting logistic regression, because the gradient descent converges much faster and the regularisation is applied evenly across features with similar scales.

segments.transcriptSnippet: Summary: logistic regression models class probabilities using the sigmoid function and log loss.
segments.transcriptText: Summary: logistic regression models class probabilities using the sigmoid function and log loss. Decision boundaries are linear. Feature engineering can handle non-linear problems. Cross-entropy loss is derived from maximum likelihood. Use precision, recall, F1 and AUC for evaluation, especially on imbalanced datasets. Softmax generalises to multi-class. Always standardise features and apply regularisation. Next session we will start on decision trees — a very different type of model that makes no linearity assumptions. See you then.

roomName: Day 3 - Decision Trees and Random Forests

hardestSegment.transcriptSnippet: Bagging, or bootstrap aggregating, is the technique Random Forest uses to reduce variance.

segments.transcriptSnippet: Decision trees are a completely different approach to machine learning from the linear models we studied last week.
segments.transcriptText: Decision trees are a completely different approach to machine learning from the linear models we studied last week. Instead of learning a weighted combination of features, a decision tree learns a sequence of if-then rules that partition the feature space into rectangular regions. Each internal node in the tree tests a single feature with a threshold. The left branch is taken if the feature value is below the threshold; the right branch if it is above. Each leaf node stores a prediction — the most common class in that leaf for classification, or the mean output for regression. Decision trees are highly interpretable: you can trace the path from the root to a leaf and understand exactly why the model made a prediction. They also require no feature scaling and can handle a mix of numerical and categorical features.

segments.transcriptSnippet: To build a decision tree we need a criterion for choosing which feature and threshold to split on at each node.
segments.transcriptText: To build a decision tree we need a criterion for choosing which feature and threshold to split on at each node. For classification, the two most common criteria are Gini impurity and information gain based on entropy. Gini impurity of a node is 1 minus the sum of squared class proportions. A pure node — where all examples belong to the same class — has Gini impurity zero. A maximally impure node — where classes are equally represented — has the highest Gini impurity. Information gain is 1 minus the entropy, where entropy is the sum of negative p times log p over all classes. At each node, we try every possible feature and every possible threshold, compute the Gini impurity or entropy of the resulting split, and choose the split that gives the greatest reduction in impurity. This greedy approach does not guarantee a globally optimal tree but works well in practice.

segments.transcriptSnippet: A fully grown decision tree will almost always overfit the training data.
segments.transcriptText: A fully grown decision tree will almost always overfit the training data. If we keep splitting until every leaf is pure, the tree will perfectly classify the training data but will fail on new examples because it has memorised noise in the training set. The standard solution is to limit the depth of the tree — the maximum number of splits from the root to a leaf. A shallow tree is less expressive but generalises better. Other hyperparameters that control tree complexity include the minimum number of samples required to split a node, the minimum number of samples in a leaf, and the maximum number of leaf nodes. All of these are regularisation techniques for decision trees. We choose these hyperparameters using cross-validation on a held-out validation set.

segments.transcriptSnippet: Feature importance in decision trees measures how much each feature contributes to reducing impurity across all splits.
segments.transcriptText: Feature importance in decision trees measures how much each feature contributes to reducing impurity across all splits. For each feature, we sum the weighted impurity reduction across all nodes where that feature was used to split, weighting by the fraction of training examples reaching that node. We then normalise so that all importances sum to one. Feature importance gives a useful signal for feature selection — low importance features may be safely removed without hurting model performance. However, decision tree feature importances can be biased: features with many possible split thresholds — such as continuous features or high-cardinality categoricals — tend to receive higher importance scores because there are more opportunities for them to be selected. This is a known limitation to be aware of when interpreting the importances.

segments.transcriptSnippet: Ensemble methods combine many weak models to produce a stronger model.
segments.transcriptText: Ensemble methods combine many weak models to produce a stronger model. A weak model is one that performs only slightly better than random guessing. The key insight is that errors made by different weak models are often uncorrelated — one model gets example A wrong but example B right, while another model gets example B wrong but example A right. When we average their predictions, the errors cancel out and the combined prediction is better than any individual model. This is the wisdom of crowds principle applied to machine learning. There are two main families of ensemble methods: bagging, which trains models independently and averages their predictions; and boosting, which trains models sequentially, with each new model focused on the examples the previous models got wrong. Random Forest is the most prominent bagging method; Gradient Boosting is the most prominent boosting method.

segments.transcriptSnippet: Random Forest builds many decision trees, each trained on a random bootstrap sample of the data.
segments.transcriptText: Random Forest builds many decision trees, each trained on a random bootstrap sample of the data. Bootstrap sampling means we randomly draw examples with replacement from the training set, creating a new dataset of the same size as the original. Because we sample with replacement, on average about 63 percent of the original examples appear in each bootstrap sample, and the remaining 37 percent — called the out-of-bag examples — are left out. For a classification problem, the final prediction is the majority vote across all trees; for regression it is the average. The out-of-bag examples can be used to estimate the generalisation error without needing a separate validation set — this is called the out-of-bag score.

segments.transcriptSnippet: Bagging, or bootstrap aggregating, reduces variance. But alone it is not enough because the trees are correlated.
segments.transcriptText: Bagging, or bootstrap aggregating, reduces variance. But alone it is not enough because the trees trained on bootstrap samples of the same dataset will tend to be correlated — they will all make similar splits at the top of the tree because the most informative features dominate. Random Forest breaks this correlation by introducing randomness in the feature selection at each split: instead of considering all features, each node only considers a random subset of features — typically the square root of the total number of features for classification. This forces different trees to use different features, decorrelating them and further reducing variance. The combination of bootstrap sampling of rows and random sampling of features at each split is what makes Random Forest particularly powerful and hard to overfit.

segments.transcriptSnippet: Gradient Boosting builds trees sequentially, each correcting the mistakes of the previous ones.
segments.transcriptText: Gradient Boosting builds trees sequentially, each correcting the mistakes of the previous ones. The first model predicts the mean of the target. The second model is trained on the residuals — the differences between the true targets and the first model's predictions. The third model is trained on the residuals of the combined first and second model, and so on. At each step we add a new tree multiplied by a learning rate — a small number like 0.1 — to slowly improve the combined model. Using a small learning rate requires more trees but tends to generalise better. Popular implementations include XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost. Gradient boosting with careful tuning often outperforms Random Forest on tabular data, but is more prone to overfitting and has more hyperparameters to tune.

segments.transcriptSnippet: When to use a tree-based model versus a linear model is an important practical question.
segments.transcriptText: When to use a tree-based model versus a linear model is an important practical question. Tree-based models — especially Random Forest and Gradient Boosting — handle non-linear relationships and feature interactions automatically, without feature engineering. They are robust to outliers and irrelevant features. However, they are harder to interpret than a single decision tree or a logistic regression, and they are slower to train and predict. Linear models are faster, more interpretable, and better calibrated. They excel when the true relationship is approximately linear. A practical heuristic: start with a linear model as a baseline. If it is not good enough, try gradient boosting. Only switch to deep learning if you have very large datasets, unstructured data like images or text, or if gradient boosting still falls short.

segments.transcriptSnippet: Wrapping up — next session we move to neural networks and deep learning.
segments.transcriptText: Wrapping up — next session we move to neural networks and deep learning. Today we covered: decision trees split the feature space using greedy impurity reduction; they overfit easily and need regularisation via max depth; Random Forest decorrelates trees using bootstrap sampling and random feature subsets; Gradient Boosting trains trees sequentially on residuals. Remember that ensemble methods almost always outperform a single model. Please revise the code examples on the course portal before next class.
